comment_text: Swing highs, Equal highs, & Trendlines hold huge liquidity same for lows. That’s why it’s best to only enter after the they get swept. When you see equal lows below Demand, place a limit order at the equal low. If you know price wicks equal lows then you have a safe systematic entry model. If price only taps the demand imbalance but doesn’t wick the equal, lows and continues to go bullish, then delete your order and come again tomorrow. It may not wick your entry in the trade a few times before hitting your TP but when it does, you’ll have the cheapest price to sell for a huge profit.

RETESTING THE EXTREME ZONE & THE LOGIC BEHIND BANK MOVEMENTS

The market didn’t revisit the extreme zone by accident—it returned to close a banking order that was positioned around the 50% mark of a wick. On the lower timeframes, we can spot liquidity within the wick, but on the higher timeframes, like the Daily, the story becomes clearer: the market shifted direction and formed a new Higher High (HH).

Here's the key: the market always pulls back to the last order that pushed it forward—the one that caused the recent HH or LL—before continuing the move. That’s why we must analyze higher timeframes first and then fine-tune entries on lower ones. Only when we combine both can we see the true narrative unfold.

Meanwhile, banks continuously bait retail traders, luring them into traps to collect the liquidity they need for their next move—one that’s often already telegraphed on the higher timeframes.

Follow the money—not the noise. Play their game—but play it against them.
